title: Dynamical mean-field theory for associative memory with block-correlated patterns
abstract: In associative memories storing correlated patterns, retrieval of individual memories can compete with symmetric mixed states. A dynamical description is needed to determine how the initial state selects between these outcomes. We extend the generating-functional dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for independent patterns to independent blocks of correlated binary patterns of fixed finite size. The resulting effective single-neuron process has a self-consistent cross-talk noise covariance and self-feedback coefficients that depend on the block-covariance eigenvalues. For hierarchically correlated patterns with nonmonotonic transfer, increasing the loading can permit retrieval from an imperfect initial state before further loading prevents it. DMFT reproduces the retrieval trajectories and basin geometry found in direct simulations. Near the lower boundary of this re-entrant region, direct networks reveal stationary saddles separating coexisting mixed and target-retrieval states. Parameter sensitivities of DMFT trajectories predict nearby shifts of this boundary. At the tested upper boundary, retrieval remains accessible from initial states with larger target overlap, indicating a change in basin access. Under fixed-point convergence assumptions, the theory recovers the equations of generalized self-consistent signal-to-noise analysis.
summary: This paper extends Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) to analyze associative memories storing correlated patterns. It determines the dynamics governing the selection between mixed and target retrieval states by deriving self-consistent equations for noise and feedback. The work shows that DMFT accurately predicts the complex retrieval boundaries and trajectories observed in simulations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the dynamical selection process among coexisting mixed states and target retrieval states in associative memories that store correlated patterns.
main_result: The Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) successfully reproduces the retrieval trajectories and basin geometry observed in direct simulations, particularly detailing how correlations affect the retrieval boundary.
method: The authors extend DMFT, originally for independent patterns, to handle blocks of correlated binary patterns by analyzing the generating functional and deriving self-consistent equations for noise covariance and feedback coefficients.
model_or_system: The system is an associative memory modeled by recurrent neural networks storing correlated binary patterns. The analysis uses the DMFT framework to derive effective single-neuron dynamics.

paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of setting up the model, deriving the extended DMFT equations, comparing the theoretical predictions with direct simulations, and summarizing the findings regarding retrieval dynamics.
why_interesting: The use of advanced mean-field techniques (DMFT) to analyze complex, non-equilibrium dynamics in a system exhibiting glassy behavior (associative memory) provides theoretical tools applicable to understanding complex many-body dynamics in disordered quantum systems.
